title: Defining relative clauses
objectives: Identify the role of a relative pronoun.
Use defining clauses to identify people and things.
Omit an object relative pronoun where appropriate.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A defining relative clause gives information needed to identify which person or thing we mean. In ‘The student who sits by the window is Maya’, who sits by the window identifies the student. Without it, the listener may not know which student we are discussing. A defining clause comes immediately after the noun it describes.

Relative words connect the clause to that noun. We commonly use who or that for people and which or that for things: ‘the woman who teaches us’ and ‘the book that I borrowed’. Where can refer to a place: ‘the café where we met’. Whose expresses a relationship or possession: ‘the student whose bag was lost’.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: A relative pronoun can be the subject of its clause: ‘The woman who lives next door is a doctor’. Who is the subject of lives, so we do not add another subject: not ‘the woman who she lives’. The relative pronoun must remain when it is the subject in this basic pattern.

The relative pronoun can also be the object: ‘The book that I borrowed is interesting’. I is the subject of borrowed and that refers to the object. In defining clauses, we can often leave out an object relative pronoun: ‘The book I borrowed is interesting’. We cannot normally leave out who in ‘the woman who lives next door’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘The people who work on Fridays’ with ‘The people who I met on Friday’. In the first clause, who is the subject of work. In the second, I is the subject of met, and who refers to the people I met. In informal English the object who can often be omitted: ‘The people I met on Friday’.

A defining clause is normally written without commas. It identifies or restricts the noun: ‘Students who have tickets may enter’ means the students with tickets may enter; it does not necessarily include all students. The next unit looks at clauses that add extra information and use commas.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not repeat the object after a relative pronoun: say ‘the book that I bought’, not ‘the book that I bought it’. In the second version, that already refers to the book, so it is an unnecessary extra object. Similarly, say ‘the woman who lives here’, not ‘the woman who she lives here’.

Who and that can both be possible for people in defining clauses, and which and that can both be possible for things. Choose according to the context or the instruction in a question. Whom occurs as an object form for people, especially in formal English, but who or an omitted object pronoun is common in everyday English.

examples.note: Who is the subject of sits.

examples.note: The object relative pronoun is omitted.

examples.note: Who identifies the people and is the subject of work.

examples.note: Whose connects the student with the bag.

examples.note: The clause identifies the relevant students.

common_errors.incorrect: The woman who she lives here is a doctor.
common_errors.correct: The woman who lives here is a doctor.
common_errors.reason: Who already functions as the subject.

common_errors.incorrect: The book that I bought it is new.
common_errors.correct: The book that I bought is new.
common_errors.reason: That already refers to the object.

common_errors.incorrect: The person lives here is a teacher.
common_errors.correct: The person who lives here is a teacher.
common_errors.reason: The subject relative pronoun is needed in this pattern.

summary: A defining relative clause identifies the noun and normally has no commas.
A subject relative pronoun stays; an object relative pronoun can often be omitted.
Who or that can refer to people; which or that can refer to things.
